subtopics: Browser-based requests for simple GET endpoints

learning_outcomes: Explain the purpose and terminology of API Clients and Endpoint Verification.
Apply or interpret one Express.js 5 pattern related to browser-based requests for simple get endpoints.
Identify a meaningful edge case and choose a repeatable local test for it.

content.intro: In this lesson, you will learn api clients and endpoint verification and connect the named syllabus points to a small Express.js example. The course baseline is Express 5.x on a supported Node.js LTS release; the page shows reference output, not execution of Node.js code.
content.why_it_matters: API Clients and Endpoint Verification matters because it helps keep the request/response contract explicit and the application maintainable as inputs, users and dependencies become less predictable. Resource-oriented HTTP APIs.

content_blocks.title: Core idea
content_blocks.text: API Clients and Endpoint Verification is part of building rest apis with express.js. Model API paths around resources and align method/status-code semantics with the operation. Use consistent response envelopes, versioning, CORS configuration, idempotency where appropriate, and API documentation. For this topic, make the observable behavior explicit, then check what happens when an input is missing, malformed, unauthorized, or a dependency fails (choose the relevant cases for this lesson).

items.title: Browser-based requests for simple GET endpoints
items.text: Treat the HTTP method and path as an API contract. Use the current Express 5 path syntax, validate captured values, and test both matching and non-matching requests.

items.title: Testing tools such as Postman or Insomnia
items.text: Make behavior reproducible with assertions for a normal case, invalid input, boundary values and errors. Mock external side effects in unit tests and keep separate integration checks for real boundaries.

items.title: Command-line HTTP clients
items.text: Keep the interface predictable for its client: use clear resource boundaries, explicit request/response formats, correct status codes, validation and tests for failure cases.

items.title: Testing headers, payloads, and status codes
items.text: Choose a status code and method that match the operation result. Semantics matter to clients and retries; never report success when work failed or remains incomplete.

items.title: Reproducing and documenting API failures
items.text: Normalize expected failures into safe, predictable responses and forward unexpected failures to the final error handler. Keep diagnostic details in protected logs, not public responses.

content_blocks.title: Read the example carefully
content_blocks.text: A useful way to study api clients and endpoint verification is to start from the first syllabus point — browser-based requests for simple get endpoints — and follow it through a small request or application example. Keep Express's built-in behavior separate from optional packages and your own application policy.

content.task: Try it yourself: adapt the worked example to demonstrate api clients and endpoint verification. Write down the exact request or command, expected status/body, one boundary case, and how you would reset the local lab. CodeLeaf does not execute Express code in this lesson page; run Node.js server examples locally.
task_acceptance_criteria: The example has a clear local run or inspection path and the required dependencies are named.
A normal request and a malformed/edge/failure request have documented expected outcomes.
No credentials, production data, or claim of successful runtime execution is included.
hints: Hint 1: identify which part of api clients and endpoint verification is supplied by Express and which part belongs to your own application or another package.
Hint 2: check the official Express 5 guide/API reference and isolate the smallest example that proves one behavior.
Hint 3: verify a success case, a boundary case and the expected status/response; restart from a clean state before repeating.
content.solution_notes: Suggested approach: Model API paths around resources and align method/status-code semantics with the operation. Use consistent response envelopes, versioning, CORS configuration, idempotency where appropriate, and API documentation. The sample is a focused reference fragment. Review all dependency, schema, proxy and runtime assumptions before using it in an application.

common_mistakes.problem: Copying an example without checking its assumptions
common_mistakes.why: A fragment may omit route setup, middleware order, external packages, database schema or production configuration.
common_mistakes.fix: State the runtime/dependency assumptions, run the focused example locally, and test a success path plus one failure path.

common_mistakes.problem: Treating all request values as trusted
common_mistakes.why: Parameters, query values, body properties, files and upstream responses can be missing or malicious.
common_mistakes.fix: Validate schema, type and bounds at the boundary; keep authorization and database constraints as separate checks.

common_mistakes.problem: Assuming the demo output means the server executed
common_mistakes.why: The course page shows reference output for Node.js/Express code; it is not an isolated Node runtime.
common_mistakes.fix: Run the example locally with the documented Node.js version and record actual command/output and test results.

summary: Explain the central idea behind api clients and endpoint verification.
Connect the relevant subtopics to the request/response or application boundary.
Verify one normal outcome and one edge/error case with repeatable evidence.
run_instructions: Open a terminal in the lesson lab directory.
Install dependencies for the sample if required; use a supported Node.js LTS release.
Run the documented file with node, send the stated request with curl or an API client, and compare the actual status/body with the reference.
reset_steps: Stop the local process with Ctrl+C.
Clear only temporary/synthetic records or files created by the lab.
Restart the server before repeating the example.
troubleshooting: If node reports a module-syntax error, check package.json module type or use the matching CommonJS syntax.
If a package cannot be resolved, install the named dependency in the local lab and verify the lockfile.
If output differs, verify middleware order, the request path/method, environment variables and the expected runtime version.
